title: The weakest part of an agent sandbox is the yes button
dek: Researchers got coding agents to steer users into broad "always allow" rules in 58% of runs. Also: a macOS test build that blanks OpenGL windows, Steam handing its deal slots to an algorithm, and sound grown from plant-growth rules.

theme.mood: a sharp Monday about who gets to say yes

tldr.text: A booby-trapped repo got coding agents to ask for a broad allow rule in **58% of runs**; once a user approved it, the hidden goal ran silently in 47 of 58 cases.
The macOS 15.8.2 release candidate leaves **window-attached OpenGL views blank**, hitting Godot and other tools. Test Mac builds before it ships.
Steam is retiring its hand-picked Daily, Midweek and Weekend Deals; in Valve's tests the personalised replacement showed **10 times more games** per user each day.
Geoffrey Huntley proposes open source that is **closed to pull requests and open to remix**: publish the intent and the patch, and let agents port it.

blocks.title: One yes can switch the sandbox off
blocks.gist: Researchers showed that a booby-trapped project can make a coding agent ask its user for a broad standing permission, and once the user agrees, the attacker's later commands run without any warning.
blocks.takeaway: A standing allow rule is a security decision, not a convenience click. Read the pattern it grants and refuse anything broader than the action in front of you.
body: Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex CLI run inside a harness that stops and asks before risky actions, like downloading from the internet. To cut down on prompts, the harness lets you approve a reusable rule instead of one action: yes, and allow similar commands from now on.

The researchers planted ordinary-looking material in a repository: failing test scripts, misleading hints in the README, a neat list of commands to run. Given a routine task, the agent ran into it and asked for a broad rule, such as allowing any `curl` command. A user who said yes had also approved everything the attacker needed later.

Across Claude Code and Codex CLI with four model setups, agents asked for the attacker's target rule in **58% of runs**. When the rule was approved, the hidden goal completed silently in 47 of 58 eligible cases (81%).

stat.label: of runs where the agent asked for the attacker's rule

blocks.why: Every agent tool that offers "don't ask again" has this weak point, and the person approving is the last check. Fewer, narrower rules cost a few more prompts and close it.
blocks.forYou: Your unattended routines live on saved allow rules. Run `/permissions` in every repo they touch and cut curl, wget, interpreter and wildcard npm rules down to exact commands; the Try this below is the checklist.

terms.def: The program around an AI model that runs its tools, enforces permissions and asks the user before risky steps.
A fenced-off environment that limits what a program can touch, such as files outside a folder or the network.
A saved permission that lets an agent run matching actions without asking again.
A command-line tool that downloads or sends data over the web, often used to fetch and run scripts.

deep: The paper, From Approval to Abuse (arXiv 2610.22987, submitted October 16), builds the attack with four cooperating agents: a planner, a builder that writes the trap repo, a proxy that plays the victim agent, and a critic. The tested setups were Codex CLI with gpt-5.6-luna and gpt-5.6-sol, and Claude Code with claude-haiku-4.5 and claude-sonnet-5.

The approved rules covered 56.9% of the category-specific capability tests the authors ran, which measures how much an attacker could do with them. The paper is an attack study: it proposes no fix of its own, and argues that harnesses should judge a rule by its scope and its consequences after approval, citing strict-policy systems such as Progent and CapScope.

nodes.label: Trap repo
nodes.note: failing tests, README hints, a tidy list of commands

nodes.label: Routine task
nodes.note: the agent works on an ordinary request and reads the trap

nodes.label: Broad rule
nodes.note: the agent asks to allow, say, any curl command

nodes.label: User says yes
nodes.note: yes, and allow similar commands from now on

nodes.label: Silent abuse
nodes.note: later harmful commands match the rule and run unasked

diagram.caption: The attack path described in From Approval to Abuse (arXiv 2610.22987). The user's approval is the step it depends on.

blocks.title: A macOS test build blanks OpenGL windows
blocks.gist: The release candidate of a small macOS Sequoia update stops older OpenGL graphics from drawing into app windows, so Godot and several desktop tools show an empty window.
blocks.background: OpenGL is an older graphics interface that Apple deprecated years ago but still ships; many engines and tools keep it as a fallback renderer.
blocks.intro: Reports on Apple's developer forum cover both release candidates of macOS 15.8.2, on Apple Silicon and under Rosetta. Apple has filed the bug and given no fix date.

steps.title: Test on the candidate
steps.text: Run your Mac build, or any OpenGL tool you depend on, on macOS 15.8.2 RC2 (build 24H225). A blank window is the symptom.

steps.title: Confirm the cause
steps.text: In your own code, the window's default framebuffer reports `GL_FRAMEBUFFER_UNDEFINED` (0x8219) and the context has no drawable. Offscreen rendering still works.

steps.title: Route around it
steps.text: Developers in the thread report that drawing through a `CAOpenGLLayer`, or rendering offscreen and presenting the result through a Core Animation layer, still works.

steps.title: Watch the bug
steps.text: Apple's report is FB25133383. Release notes for the update mention only security fixes, so check each new candidate.

blocks.why: A point update aimed at security fixes can still break rendering for players. Anything that falls back to OpenGL on Mac, including Godot's compatibility renderer, is exposed.
blocks.forYou: If a three.js wrapper or Godot export of the browser games ships a Mac desktop build, check which renderer it uses; WebGL in a browser is not the path reported broken.

terms.def: A build the vendor expects to ship unless a serious bug turns up; RC for short.
The block of memory a graphics program draws a frame into before it reaches the screen.
Apple's translator that runs apps built for Intel chips on Apple Silicon Macs.

deep: Reported details: `kCGLCPHasDrawable` returns 0, `CGLSetSurface` returns `kCGLBadDrawable` (10005) and the kernel log shows "Invalid surface ID". `NSOpenGLView` and `NSOpenGLContext setView:` render nothing; `CAOpenGLLayer`, `NSOpenGLLayer` and offscreen framebuffers still work. Reports name Godot, Alacritty, kitty, FreeCAD, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer and Bambu Studio among affected apps, on M1 and M4 machines. A second report is FB25171330.
9to5Mac dates RC1 to October 7 and RC2 to October 13. Whether macOS 26.7.2 candidates are affected is not confirmed.

blocks.title: A kit that lets coding agents read compiled programs
blocks.gist: An open-source project connects coding agents to the tools experts use to take apart compiled software, so the agent can study a binary and test its guesses in a loop.
blocks.name: Reverse Engineer Anything
blocks.what: MCP servers that hand Ghidra, Hopper and IDA to Claude Code and Codex, running on your own machine.
body: The agent queries disassembly, follows references between functions and checks its theories against the binary. The project also handles Electron apps and .NET assemblies, and says plainly that it does not recover original source code. One showcase rebuilt a sound-panning function from the game DX-Ball until it matched all 3,205 test cases on x86.
Developers on Hacker News asked what it adds over telling an agent to use Ghidra directly, and others raised worries about copying games and bypassing paywalls.

facts.v: Claude Code and Codex, through MCP

blocks.why: Reading compiled code used to take a specialist and weeks. Packaged for agents, it is within reach of anyone, which helps porting and debugging and lowers the cost of copying shipped work.
blocks.forYou: Assume compiled plugin binaries can now be read by agents with little effort; keep anything you need to protect on a server or behind licence checks, not in obscurity.

terms.def: Model Context Protocol, a standard way to plug tools and data into an AI agent.
A free tool from the NSA for taking apart compiled programs.
A long-established commercial disassembler used by security researchers.
A compiled program turned back into readable machine instructions.

image.alt: REA investigation flow: ask your agent about a local target, REA inspects and traces through CLI or MCP with local analysis tools, you read the evidence, and your agent explains, implements or tests.

blocks.title: Four notes from people who run agents all day
blocks.gist: Geoffrey Huntley's write-up of a conversation with Armin Ronacher and others is full of first-hand numbers on what heavy agent use costs and which habits are changing.
blocks.intro: From "state of agentic coding #11", published October 16. The figures are the speakers' own estimates.

items.title: Regenerate your agent instructions after each model release
items.text: The speakers delete and rewrite their AGENTS.md files and skills when a new model ships, because advice written for the last model can hold the new one back.

items.title: Models are skipping the edit tool
items.text: With the latest models, the dedicated edit tool in the Pi agent went unused in about 80% of cases; the models wrote code to make changes instead.

items.title: A live runtime with two tools
items.text: Huntley connected a model to a running Lisp image with only two tools, evaluate and define. Changes apply live with no files, build or CI, and roll back by generation.

items.title: The real token bill
items.text: Ronacher's car display adapter took about $20 of hardware and about $15,000 of tokens. Huntley estimates his own use would cost over $200,000 a month at list prices.

blocks.why: These are working habits from people who publish what they do, and the first one costs nothing to adopt: instructions age as fast as the models they were written for.
blocks.forYou: Put a note in the routine and skills docs to re-read and prune them when the next Claude model ships, and test one routine with its instructions cut in half.

terms.def: A file in a repository with standing instructions for coding agents.
Packaged instructions and scripts an agent loads when a task needs them.
A running Lisp program whose code and state can be changed while it runs.

sources.label: Geoffrey Huntley: state of agentic coding #11

blocks.title: DeepSeek sells web search to agents by the request
blocks.gist: DeepSeek now offers simple web search and page-reading services that any agent can call, priced per successful request.
body: Search returns ranked results; Fetch returns a page as Markdown. Only responses with content are billed, and billing starts November 1. Calls made through Claude Code, Codex or DeepSeek's own harness are free for now.
blocks.why: Cheap, plain search and fetch services make it easier to give a home-built agent the web without running a scraper.
blocks.forYou: A candidate web tool for a self-built routine outside Claude Code; check its rate limit of 5 requests a second before relying on it.

terms.def: A plain-text format with light markup for headings, links and lists.

deep: Endpoints: POST /v1/tools/search (query of 1 to 128 characters, 1 to 50 results, with site, language, phrase, exclusion and date operators) and POST /v1/tools/fetch (URLs up to 8,192 characters). Each result carries a relevance score from 0 to 3 and an authority tier from 0 to 4. Limits are 5 requests a second per account per API, plus a per-domain limit on Fetch; over the limit returns HTTP 429. Billing starts at midnight Beijing time on November 1.

sources.label: DeepSeek API docs: search and fetch

blocks.title: Closed to pull requests, open to remix
blocks.gist: Geoffrey Huntley argues that when agents make code cheap, reviewing strangers' contributions stops being worth it, and proposes publishing the idea and the patch for others to adapt instead.
blocks.intro: Huntley has turned off pull requests on his own releases and kept discussions open. His example builds each change as a Nix overlay: a small patch, written once, that applies on top of a package everywhere it is used.

rows.left: A change you ask the maintainer to merge
rows.right: Source plus a clear statement of intent, offered as is
Nobody upstream; whoever remixes owns their copy
Each remixer, with no duty on the author
One overlay reused in dev shells, Docker images, CI and agent sandboxes
Agents scan the fork network and summarise remixes

blocks.verdict: An opinion with a working demo, not a trend yet. It names a real cost: when code is cheap to write, a maintainer's review time is the scarce part.
blocks.why: Maintainers are already drowning in low-effort, machine-written contributions. Shipping intent and patches instead of accepting merges is one way to keep a project healthy.
blocks.forYou: For marketplace plugins, a public sample or extension point plus clear intent may serve buyers better than accepting outside patches you then have to support.

terms.def: Proposed changes someone asks a project's maintainers to review and merge.
A small file in the Nix packaging system that modifies a package without forking it.
GitHub's map of every copy made from a repository.

deep: The demo repository is ghuntley/nix-demo. One example overlay patches Git so it refuses force pushes, and the same overlay is reused across development shells, Docker images, NixOS machines, CI and agent sandboxes without maintaining a fork.

sources.label: Geoffrey Huntley: a new model for open source

blocks.title: Steam's deal slots go personal
blocks.gist: Valve is replacing the hand-picked daily and weekend deals on Steam with discounts chosen for each player, so a sale no longer depends on winning a slot.

stats.label: more games shown per user each day in Valve's tests

body: Valve announced it on September 29; booked slots still run. The replacement, driven by each player's history and wishlist, arrives in early 2027 with new tools for studios to manage discounts.
blocks.why: A small game used to wait for a rare curated slot. Under the new system, wishlists and a player's own interests decide who sees a discount.
blocks.forYou: Plan launch-year discounts around wishlist growth rather than a featured slot, and watch for Valve's new discount tools early next year.

terms.def: A player's saved list of games they want, which Steam uses to notify them of releases and sales.

sources.label: Inven Global: Steam to end the curated calendar

blocks.title: Fab adds bundles and complete UEFN systems
blocks.gist: Epic's asset store Fab now sells bundles of products in one purchase, and a new kind of listing: complete, editable game systems that open straight in Fortnite's editor.
blocks.background: Fab is Epic's marketplace for Unreal Engine and Fortnite assets; UEFN is Unreal Editor for Fortnite, the tool for building islands inside Fortnite.
blocks.name: Fab bundles
blocks.what: Several Fab products added to your library in one purchase, launched alongside UEFN source assets.
body: UEFN source assets are working systems rather than reference files: AI and NPC behaviours, vehicles, weapons, interface and environments, many built with Verse and Scene Graph. Epic offers a free starter kit and lists them through Fab's UEFN integration. The announcement does not cover bundle pricing or who can create bundles.
blocks.why: Bundles give sellers a way to package related tools, and complete systems for Fortnite creators open a new kind of product on the same store.
blocks.forYou: Bundles fit modular plugins sold together, such as combat with inventory; check the seller docs for bundle rules before planning prices. A Verse version of one system could reach UEFN creators.

terms.def: Epic's programming language for scripting gameplay in Fortnite islands.
Epic's newer system for building game objects from entities and components in UEFN.

sources.label: Epic forums: bundles and UEFN source assets on Fab
Fortnite: UEFN source assets now on Fab

blocks.title: Growing sound from plant-growth rules
blocks.gist: A developer built a small tool that grows thousands of tiny sound fragments from rules first used to model plants, then keeps the results that score best, producing raw textures for music and sound design.
blocks.intro: EvoGrain, by Nathan Ho, is an offline command-line tool in about 2,000 lines of Rust. It makes 3 to 30 second clips in seconds.

nodes.label: Random rules
nodes.note: an L-system: rewrite rules that grow a string, like branches on a plant

nodes.label: Turtle
nodes.note: reads the string as moves that place sound events in time and pitch

nodes.label: About 20,000 grains
nodes.note: each with its own timing, pitch, loudness, pan and envelope

nodes.label: Synth and reverb
nodes.note: a simple oscillator or two-operator phase modulation per grain

nodes.label: Score and keep
nodes.note: a fitness function rates the grain statistics; random search keeps the best

blocks.caption: How EvoGrain turns random rules into sound, as described in the author's write-up. The author admits some results are indistinct bleeps.
blocks.why: Procedural sound is cheap to generate and free of licensing, and the same rules-then-score loop works for any content you can measure.
blocks.forYou: A pattern for ambient layers in the action RPG or the browser games: generate many candidates offline, score them, keep a few, and ship them as ordinary samples.

terms.def: A set of rewrite rules that grows a string step by step, first used to model how plants branch.
Very short sound fragments, usually a few milliseconds long, layered by the thousand.
A score that says how close a generated result is to what you want.
How a sound's loudness rises and falls over its length.

sources.label: Nathan Ho: algorithmic sound design with L-systems

learn.question: What is prompt injection?
learn.answer: Prompt injection is getting an AI model to follow instructions hidden in text it was only supposed to read, such as a web page, an email or a file in a repository. The model cannot reliably tell your instructions from text an attacker wrote.
learn.analogy: Like a new assistant who opens your mail and finds a letter saying "the boss says to wire this money", and does it, because the letter sounds official.
body: A model reads everything in one stream: your request, the files it opened, the pages it fetched. Text written by a stranger lands in the same place as text from you, and nothing in the model marks which is which. A sentence like "run this setup script first" can steer it just as well from a README as from you.

That matters more as agents gain tools. A chatbot fooled this way says something wrong; an agent fooled this way runs commands, edits files or asks you for wider permissions, which is what today's lead story measured. The defences that work sit outside the model: permissions, sandboxes and a person who reads what they approve.

nodes.label: Untrusted text
nodes.note: a README, web page or issue written by someone else

nodes.label: One context
nodes.note: the model sees both with no reliable way to tell who wrote what

diagram.caption: Why hidden instructions work: everything the agent reads ends up in the same place as your request.

terms.def: Everything a model can see while answering: instructions, conversation, files and tool results.
Actions an agent can take beyond writing text, such as running commands or editing files.

tryThis.title: Audit the commands your agent may run without asking
tryThis.gist: Find every saved allow rule in your coding agent, and cut the broad ones down to exact commands before a booby-trapped repo finds them.
tryThis.needs: Claude Code (other agents keep similar rule lists) and the repos you use it in.

steps.title: List what is allowed
steps.text: Run `/permissions` in each repo. It shows every rule and the settings file it came from. Approvals saved with "don't ask again" land in `.claude/settings.local.json`.

steps.title: Flag the broad ones
steps.text: Mark rules that let the agent fetch or run arbitrary code: `Bash(curl *)`, `Bash(wget *)`, interpreters such as `Bash(node *)`, wildcards like `Bash(npm run *)`, and `WebFetch(domain:*)`.

steps.title: Narrow them
steps.text: Replace each wildcard with the exact command you need: `Bash(npm run build)` matches only that command. Allow web fetches per domain instead of everywhere.

steps.title: Deny the network tools
steps.text: The docs suggest denying curl and wget in Bash and using the fetch tool with per-domain rules. Deny rules win over allow rules, whatever their order.

tryThis.check: `/permissions` lists no rule that would let the agent download and run something unseen, and asking the agent to curl a URL is refused instead of running.

terms.def: A `*` in a rule that matches anything in that position.

tryThis.forYou: Start with the radar repo and any repo a scheduled routine runs in, since nobody is there to read a prompt when they run.

Lobsters retired its vibecoding tag, added ai-tooling for stories about building AI tools, and now treats content without meaningful human authorship as spam.
Dominik Picheta built KillSwitch, a language designed to trip up LLMs; in his own tests the best score, 66.8, went to Claude Opus 5, and he says it does not prove understanding.
Meta's Sapienz, which found 558 unknown crashes in 1,000 Android apps in 2016, won ISSTA's most influential paper award; it now runs millions of tests a day at Meta.
Meta's open-weight Muse Spark Open is reported at 816B total and 42B active parameters with a 1M-token context, under a custom licence that is not open source.
Cloudflare's Local Explorer can now fire a Worker's scheduled handler on demand during local development, so cron jobs can be tested without waiting.
Cloudflare's cf CLI beta moves its command names to kebab-case, a breaking change for scripts, and adds a docs search command.
Codex Desktop on older macOS versions can fill its Crashpad pending folder with dump files, by some reports past 170 GB; the issue is open with no fix.

sparks.title: Sphinx: a quiz before you push agent code
sparks.signal: 243 points and 85 comments on Hacker News since October 18.
sparks.hook: A reviewer model that never saw your chat reads the diff and asks what the change does when things go wrong; answer right or the push waits.
sparks.borrow: The pattern more than the product: a pre-push hook that checks you understand agent-written changes. Commenters note the friction and how easy it is to paste the question into an agent.
sparks.forYou: Worth a trial on one protected branch of a SaaS repo, to see whether it catches a single real misunderstanding in a week.

sparks.title: esp32sim: microcontroller firmware running in a browser
sparks.signal: 193 points on Hacker News on October 17; 349 GitHub stars.
sparks.hook: It boots the chip's real ROM, bootloader and an unmodified app, and models screens, touch, audio and WiFi. The author, an emulator veteran, built it with Claude.
sparks.borrow: An emulator in the loop lets an agent test hardware code with no board on the desk, and the same idea fits any device or console target.
sparks.forYou: A reminder that a fast emulator or headless build is what lets an agent check its own work on a target you cannot click through.

sparks.title: The Duck Pond: quacks with no recordings
sparks.signal: 170 points and 43 comments on Hacker News on October 17.
sparks.hook: Every quack is synthesized from a physical model of a duck's voice, with distance rings for positional audio; the author says an LLM loop tuned the parameters until spectrograms matched a real recording.
sparks.borrow: Creature calls and ambience by fitting a synth to a reference sound in a loop: no sample licences and almost no memory.
sparks.forYou: Pairs with today's sound story: a tuning loop like this could produce creature voices for the action RPG.

sparks.title: Thank You Bus Driver
sparks.signal: 95% positive of 168 Steam reviews since its October 14 launch, though only 11 players were online when checked.
sparks.hook: A black-and-white bus route where a passenger's thank you is the currency and rule-breakers get slapped by long arms; the first game from Double Fine's new small-game label.
sparks.borrow: A one-palette art style and a short three-hour scope with one rule change per shift: a way to ship something odd without a big team.
sparks.forYou: A model for a small side release between big projects: tight scope, one strong look, a low price.

image.alt: Black and white cartoon view from the driver's seat of a bus: hands on the wheel, a town through the windshield, passengers in the mirror, a 02:40.84 timer and a Thank-o-meter gauge.

sparks.title: Five Hundred Clocks, all written by one model
sparks.signal: 66 points and 27 comments on Hacker News on October 18.
sparks.hook: 500 working clocks in one 6.3 MB HTML file, themes picked by Claude Opus 5.5; the author estimates about 15 million tokens.
sparks.borrow: Let the model propose the ideas and keep the human as curator. Commenters loved a few, such as a Pong clock, and found many repeats, so budget for culling.
sparks.forYou: The same approach could fill a jam-style batch of micro-games, with a hard filter on repeats.

sparks.title: HyperFrames: videos written as web pages
sparks.signal: About 66,900 stars, with 5,883 added this week on GitHub's trending page.
sparks.hook: Write a video as HTML and CSS with seekable animation, then render the same MP4 every time; it ships skills that teach coding agents the plan, preview and render loop.
sparks.borrow: Trailers, release clips and store videos generated from a page and re-rendered on every release.
sparks.forYou: A scripted product video per plugin version, rendered in CI, instead of re-recording by hand.

lab.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
lab.headline: Messier code costs more to have agents review and fix, mostly because messy code lives in bigger files.
lab.authors: Lo Gullstrand Heander, Markus Borg, Emma Söderberg et al.
lab.problem: Code review is moving to multi-agent pipelines billed per token. Does poor code quality raise that bill beyond what the size of the change explains?
lab.idea: Take 465 pull requests written by agents in 246 repositories, run the same five-agent review-and-fix pipeline on each with three different models, and model the token cost against a code quality score and the size of the change.
lab.result: Each point of CodeHealth score meant 3.5% to 6.1% fewer tokens, for all three models. Quality was unrelated to pull request size. The extra cost sat in review, where agents went round more often on unhealthy code. Adjusting for file size absorbed the effect, which the authors read as file size carrying it.
lab.useIt: If agents review your code, splitting very large files is a cost lever as well as a readability one. Measure tokens per pull request before and after a split.
lab.forYou: The large plugin source files are the first candidates: split one and compare agent review tokens on the next few changes.

lab.title: Poison Valleys: Diagnosing Path-Dependent Failure in LLM Code Repair
lab.headline: A wrong idea does more damage when it sits in an agent's plan than in its first guess about the bug.
lab.where: NeurIPS 2026 workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior
lab.problem: A failing test says a patch is wrong, not which earlier decision caused it.
lab.idea: Plant plausible but wrong technical beliefs into a model's hypothesis, its plan, or both, then trace the chain from observation to code with targeted checks. 1,844 model requests on two small Python repair tasks.
lab.result: With the experiment mix matched, moving the same misconception from the hypothesis into the plan raised failures by 32.2% on one task and 28.9% on the other. Each misconception broke requirements in its own pattern. Two small synthetic tasks, so a diagnostic result rather than a benchmark.
lab.useIt: Review an agent's plan, not only its diff: add a plan check before code is written, and when a fix fails, ask which stage went wrong first.
lab.forYou: A plan-review step before edits in long routines is cheap; try it on the next bug fix that fails twice.

lab.title: StayStill: a large-scale 3D idle animation dataset
lab.headline: A free dataset of how real people stand around, for characters that look alive while doing nothing.
lab.authors: Eneko Atxa Landa, Igor Rodriguez, Elena Lazkano et al.
lab.where: Computer Graphics Forum (Symposium on Computer Animation 2026)
lab.problem: Idle motion is what players see most, yet it is barely studied because no dedicated training data existed.
lab.idea: Record 50 non-actors standing idle with four GoPro cameras and the open-source FreeMoCap, label 18 idle actions such as checking a phone, and release an evaluation protocol and a baseline that builds idles by joining transitions.
lab.result: About 6 hours of motion (645,000 frames at 30 fps) from 50 people, with evaluation code and a pre-trained baseline. It is a dataset paper, so the contribution is the data and the protocol rather than a score.
lab.useIt: Use the clips for idle layers on NPCs, or borrow the capture recipe: four consumer cameras and free software were enough for usable data.
lab.forYou: Idle variety is cheap polish for the action RPG's NPCs; check the dataset licence before using clips in a shipped game.

image.alt: Eight grey mannequin figures standing in different idle poses: hands clasped, scratching the head, gesturing, arms crossed, leaning.
image.credit: Atxa Landa et al., Computer Graphics Forum, CC BY

note: A quiet window for engine and tool releases: no Unreal, Unity or Godot release landed since the last issue, so the Steam deals story is an older one earlier issues missed. The sweep got HTTP 403 from Reddit and some news feeds, and searches surfaced no verifiable posts from X, TikTok or YouTube.
